reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A benign tumour of brown adipose tissue, named for the fat that hibernating animals use for thermogenesis
Typically affects young to middle-aged adults and presents as a slow-growing, painless, mobile mass
Favoured sites are the interscapular region, back, neck, axilla, thigh, and mediastinum, mirroring the distribution of brown fat
The characteristic cell is a multivacuolated adipocyte with granular, eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm
The lesion is highly vascular and often intensely avid on FDG PET, which can lead to a false suspicion of malignancy
Recurrent chromosomal rearrangements affect the 11q13-21 region, distinguishing it from ordinary lipoma
On MRI it resembles fat but is typically slightly less bright than subcutaneous fat on T1 with prominent internal vascular flow voids
Marginal excision is curative and recurrence is not expected
reference.pathophysiology: Hibernoma is a benign neoplasm recapitulating brown adipose tissue, the specialised thermogenic fat abundant in the fetus and neonate and retained in adults at sites such as the interscapular region, neck, and mediastinum. The tumour cells are packed with mitochondria whose uncoupling protein activity gives the cytoplasm its granular, eosinophilic, multivacuolated appearance and accounts for the high metabolic activity seen on functional imaging. The rich capillary network reflects the high oxygen demand of thermogenic fat. Recurrent structural rearrangements of chromosome 11q13-21, including loss involving the region around the MEN1 locus, are characteristic and separate hibernoma from conventional white-fat lipomas. Despite its vascularity and metabolic avidity, the lesion is entirely benign with no capacity for local aggression or metastasis.
additionalDifferentials: Atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma
Myxoid liposarcoma when myxoid areas predominate
Rhabdomyoma or granular cell tumour on cytological grounds
Metastatic deposit or lymphoma given the PET avidity
additionalInvestigations: MRI to characterise the fatty mass and its vascularity
FDG PET awareness that avidity is expected and does not indicate malignancy
Image-guided core biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Histology demonstrating multivacuolated brown fat cells
Cytogenetic or molecular assessment for 11q rearrangements in difficult cases
Cross-sectional imaging to define the compartment before excision
redFlags: Intense metabolic avidity misinterpreted as a malignant or metastatic lesion
Rapid growth or infiltration raising concern for a liposarcoma
Mediastinal or deep location causing local mass effect
Unexpected recurrence after excision prompting review of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Hibernoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; complete marginal excision is curative and local recurrence or malignant transformation does not occur. The main clinical hazard is misinterpretation of its metabolic avidity as malignancy.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or over-treating a benign lesion because of striking FDG avidity
Confusing multivacuolated cells with the lipoblasts of liposarcoma
Underestimating intra-operative vascularity, which can cause troublesome bleeding
Failing to consider hibernoma in a fatty mass at a classic brown-fat site
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Complete marginal surgical excision as the definitive, curative treatment
Confirm benign brown-fat histology with MRI and image-guided core biopsy before excision where diagnosis is uncertain
Recognise expected FDG PET avidity as benign to avoid over-treatment as a sarcoma
Cross-sectional imaging to define the compartment and rich vascularity for surgical planning, anticipating intraoperative bleeding
Reassurance with no adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy required
Minimal follow-up, as local recurrence and malignant transformation do not occur
